utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos. Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bos: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac from your testimony yesterday, I'd like to clarify something. Is it correct that it's your position that the release of the presidential transcripts by President Mesic in the course of the year 2000, both to the media and also to the Office of the Prosecutor, that that was a violation of the then-existing Croatian legislation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if this was a violation of that legislation, why then was there a need to issue -- a need for the parliament to issue a decree in January 2001, which is Exhibit D1323 -- to transfer the recordings of these meetings to the Croatian national archives so that they would not be released publicly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian national diet, that is, at the initiative of some clubs of MPs, tried to include that question in the agenda throughout 2000. However, it -- the turn of this item came eventually towards the end of the year, and the diet then authorised the government to pass a decision that then was taken by the government. So MPs, the clubs of some MPs -- the caucuses of some MPs, including my party, which is the largest party, even though it is an opposition party, we have made it immediately known that these transcripts appeared in the media, that it should be therefore discussed and certain decisions and conclusions should be adopted in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That doesn't answer the question Mr. Bos put to you. If you let Mr. Bos ask you the question again. You didn't answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kovac, my question was: When, then, was there a need to issue such a decree? Because it's your testimony that the existing legislation was sufficient. Why was there a need to issue such a decree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We in the opposition thought that the existing laws, which were in force at the time, and the government's decision of 1999 sufficed. Sufficient regulation to regulate the matter. And we warned the current government at that time too, that laws of the Republic of Croatia were being violated. However, the ruling coalition did not go along with that immediately. But then we insisted that it be included in the agenda of the diet, and the decision of the government of the Republic of Croatia of 2001 is practically identical with the one that was issued in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it a fair statement, from what you just said, that -- that there at least was a difference of opinion on whether the existing law actually dealt -- whether -- under the existing law transcripts could be released or not. Because you're saying that it was the opposition's opinion that it was so. But were there different views on this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were different views. I repeat: We in the opposition considered those laws to be enough. However, the ruling coalition nevertheless wanted it discussed once again so that a definitive decision could be taken. And it was taken in January 2001. Yes, there were divergences, but with this decision the government has confirmed that we were right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just briefly look at Exhibit D1328, which was the law in existence in the year 2000. This is deprivation law on archives and archival materials. Now, Mr. Kovac, in your examination-in-chief you refer to Article 20 of this law. I'd like you to look at that law -- at that article again. Do you have that in front of you, Article 20?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it was your testimony that -- is it correct that it was your testimony that under this article, these presidential transcripts you have been -- not released for at least 30 years? Is that -- was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the second -- the second line of this article, which reads as follows: "Archive records are accessible before the expiry of 30 years. If such records are intended to the public, since their generation, or if it's approved by generator." Let me ask you first this: How do you read the sentence "are intended to the public"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it has been intended for the public right from the beginning, or if it is approved by the author. The law regulates which are -- which documents are not intended for the public, and these transcripts make part of such document. The -- at the moment of inception of documents, it is immediately known whether they will be intended for the public or not, so that this article prescribes how these articles are to be offered to the public for inspection or use. And the second paragraph of the same article regulates what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at that last line of the second sentence, which give it is other exception. If it's approved -- well, in the English version it says "If it's approved by a generator." Now, with regard to the presidential transcripts, who would be the generator of these presidential transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is the generator -- who might be the generator of the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this law was drafted in 1996, it simply never crossed anybody's mind that what is happening could happen. The transcripts in the president's office are the state property, that is, the property of the Republic of Croatia. This is archival documentation. These are not private transcripts of a person but the institution called the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But witness, would it not be that if you read article 20 -- would that not be the case that the generator would be the presidential office in this case, who kept the presidential archives or the presidential transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a legal entity. The President of the Republic, the institution -- the institute of the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And President Mesic, as the head of that office, would he not be entitled then to approve the release of these presidential transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally. There is a procedure to be followed, and this procedure is laid down by law, and the decision of the government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just refer to you to Article 3 in order to get a definition of the "generator." Look at Article 3. And it's a bit further after the -- after the middle part of that article. It says the following: "The creators of archive and current records are considered legal or physical persons by whose function and activity they are generated." Now, wouldn't you agree that under this provision, President Mesic would be the person -- would be the -- would be the generator in this -- in this legislation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Mesic may not be considered the generator because if that were so, then there would be a procedure under which he could release certain documents, certain transcripts, archival documentations and recordings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's leave document D1328 aside. Let's move on to document D1329, which is the law on the protection of data secrecy. Isn't it true that this law deals with the confidentiality of documents and which documents should be -- should be confidential and how they should be treated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at Article 4 of this -- of this law. Reading out the first line: "Documents containing secret data shall be visibly marked with the type of secret and the degree of secrecy." Do you read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday I provided you with document PT 12, which was one of the presidential transcripts. And I don't know if you can -- if the witness can be given that document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And maybe the -- maybe the front page of that document -- of the original document, the B/C/S document, could be put on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: , Your Honour, is there any --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I understand the French booth want a copy, but the registry only has one copy and it's used for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think we've provided copies of all exhibits yesterday. But if the French booth need an extra copy, I may be able to provide it. It will be taken care of. Mr. Usher, could we put the front page of that document on the overhead projector, please. It seems that the projector has a will of its own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, could you have a look at that front page of that document, and do you see anywhere any sign or any mark that this document is a secret document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question is a speculative one and therefore the answer can be speculative too, because the Prosecutor has not yet assured us of the authenticity of this -- of this. We have not seen the original. The original is as far as we can understand a tape from which this was taken. Where are these tapes? Whether these are original, whether these are not original, the Prosecution does not know that either. And now -- and now the Prosecutor wants the witness to look at these fragments from the transcripts, from the records, and to give an answer, which can be nothing but speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. This has nothing to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- With the original tapes. The original -- I mean, these are transcripts from the original tapes, and the existence of the original tapes and the authenticity of the document has nothing to do with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think we are only using the first page of this document, not the whole document, so I believe that -- I notice a word on the right upper corner saying that "recorded," which is a transcript from a recording, if I'm not mistaken. If -- if that is the archive document, then it should be classified a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This is not a document from the archive. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, is there any indication on this front page that this document was classified as secret?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand these thing, no, there is no such marking. It doesn't say that this is classified. But if there were tapes which were recorded and perhaps on the tapes it is marked that they should be considered confidential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like -- let's move on. And I'd like you to read Article 13 of this -- of this law. Let me read it out to you: "Heads of public bodies and authorised officials of the Republic of Croatia shall by special report, within their powers, and in compliance with the law, regulation or by law of the competent body classify the type and degree of secrecy of data and lay down special protection measures as well as the persons who shall be informed of the secret data." Now, under this article, Mr. Kovac, would President Mesic or President Tudjman, be in -- not be an authorised official of the Republic of Croatia who could actually classify these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a strictly legal matter, and I'm not a lawyer so I wouldn't know the answer to it. But it clearly transpires even from this article what this is all about. I know that President Tudjman did not delegate any powers to anyone to do it, as paragraph 2 of the same article says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it true that President Tudjman never classified these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that it would be the job of the president of the state. I'm sure there are services which do these things and which did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave that document aside and let's move on. Witness, do you know what the Republic of Croatia's obligations are to this Tribunal under the -- of Article 7 of the UN charter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia and the diet, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia, of which I was a member, propagated [As interpreted] its constitution and its law in combination with the Tribunal. And the Republic of Croatia has cooperated with The Hague Tribunal and continues to do so. Now I wouldn't really be able to quote the article that you mention, but it has to do with the cooperation with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what Croatia's obligations are of this Tribunal under the Dayton Peace Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the obligation of the Republic of Croatia as a party to the Dayton Accords and in accordance with its law in cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, the Republic of Croatia is bound to -- is obligated to cooperate with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about this law on the cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Do you know of any other step that is the Republic of Croatia took under Article 29 of the Tribunal Statute to meet its obligations to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish you could quote for me the Article 29 of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 29 of the Tribunal Statute deals with the cooperation of member states to this Tribunal. And I'll read out the article to you. "States shall cooperate with the International Tribunal in the investigation and prosecution of persons accused of committing serious violations of international humanitarian law." In the second paragraph: "States shall comply without undue delay, with any request for assistance or an order issued by a Trial Chamber, including but not limited to the identification and locations of persons, the taking of testimony and the production of evidence, service of documents, the arrest or detention of persons, and the surrender or the transfer of the accused to the International Tribunal." So my question is: Do you know what other step it is Republic of Croatia took to meet its obligations in the cooperation with this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the government office for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and it is headed by the deputy prime minister, Mr. Goran Granic, and I do not know whether they took upon themselves any additional obligations concerning the cooperation with the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're referring here to the council for cooperation with the Tribunal. And as you rightly said, the deputy prime minister, Mr. Goran Granic, is the head of this council. Now, Mr. Kovac, are you aware that this institution, this council for cooperation with the Tribunal, has produced 127 presidential transcripts to the Office of the Prosecutor since the decree of January 2001 was issued?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it not true that you're not aware of this piece of information because under the current Croatian legislation the release of presidential transcripts is in the hand of the government and not the parliament, as you've stated in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the government -- on the basis of the government decision of 2001, the government took upon itself the responsibility of disposing of these matters, but in line with the laws and the decree which had been passed in the beginning -- in the beginning of 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true, Mr. Kovac -- would you not agree with me that the release of these presidential transcripts is in fact an internal political matter for the Republic of Croatia, and that you have either politicians who are there to support -- who are supporting the release of these transcripts and politicians who are against it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a problem of the individual politician, either in position or opposition. It's a matter of strategic interest for the Republic of Croatia, and everybody has to adhere to the law passed by the Croatian diet, the parliament. And this applies both to those who agree with the handing over of the transcripts and those who do not agree with that. Law has to be respected. And I believe that in this case, the law has not been respected, and that is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that members of the HDZ gazette are particularly afraid of what will be revealed if these transcripts are being released?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Members of the HDZ are concerned because the rule of law isn't functioning. Nobody is afraid of that, what he has done during the past 12 years, neither I, myself; nor other members of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to a different topic. Yesterday I gave you document PT 12. And I think you have it in front of you again. You were given it. Did you get a chance of reading this document, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the transcript which you gave me during the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't succeed in readings it during those 30 minutes, but I just browsed through it to see who the persons involved were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's browse through this document again, and we'll do it together now. Let me first ask you. Is it not true that you were present at this meeting of which -- at this meeting which was held in the Vila Dalmacija in Split, on the 5th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday when you asked me, I said that what I've seen in the transcript, that it proves that it's not authentic and that it's false. I've seen that my name was mentioned in relation to it, but I was not in Split at all on that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're denying that you were present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as far as my memory serves me, as far as I recall, I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move, then, for the B/C/S version to page 0156965. And you will find the numbers on the right-hand corner. In the English version, it's -- it's page --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand which -- the number, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat it for you again. It's page 0156965. In the English version, it's page number 018 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just inform the Judges of the English version, Mr. Kovac. The English version is number 0182745, which is one of the last pages of the bundle. It's in fact -- on the bottom, it's page number 20. Do you have that page in front of you, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it in the bottom paragraph -- I'll read out to you what it says: "Also, I cannot but mention two men who are present here. They are Grubisic and Milan Kovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see it but it's not present there. It would be important to say to the witness who said that. From what you've given us, we cannot see who is speaking and who is saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos. Would you please help us to establish that. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's -- it's true that the transcript doesn't reveal who actually said this, because as sometimes happens with these transcripts, the transcribers would not know who the person was who was talking. And on this occasion, it was -- it was such an occasion where the person who was speaking was not identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honours, how should the witness know? I ask for seriousness, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, Mr. Krsnik, I think the Prosecutor is just trying to refresh the memory of this witness, because his name was mentioned here. Your witness may say that he cannot remember anything about it, because he was not there as we heard. And he may remember what happened on that occasion. Let us hear what the witness is going to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really truly wasn't in Split on that day and attend such a meeting, because here I can see the name of Ciro Ruzic, for example. That person doesn't exist in the political life of the Republic of Croatia or among the ranks of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And there are some other names for which I've never heard of before, and I really truly did not attend such a meeting. I always, when attending such meetings, I would be talking -- I always participated in the talks. I doubt it that I would keep silent. This is what bothers me, because it doesn't say who stated that I was present Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts there, because this is what raises my doubt that the transcripts were written, edited, in order to discredit many people and to burn them with something for which they really have -- are not responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mention --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I -- there is a deputy Kovac from Split. Maybe the first name is wrong here, but it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that Ciro Grubisic, that he didn't exist in the political life. Do you know this person Ciro Grubisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness didn't say that name. Why is the Prosecutor raising -- the witness said Ruzic, not Grubisic I don't know how it entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, try it again. Mr. Bos, try it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refer to page 16, line 19, where the witness says: "Because here I can see the name of Ciro -- and then it says Ruzic -- but in the transcript it says Grubisic, so I think this was something that simply was not picked up by the transcribers. Now, witness, do you know this man Ciro Grubisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Ciro Grubisic. He was a Croatian -- Croatian consulate in Mostar for many years, if you're referring to that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, are you saying that this man exists, but he was not an important player in Croatian political life? Is that what you meant to say? Because I was going to ask you a question about that. In other words, you accept that such a person exists, but is it your evidence that he wasn't an important political player?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ciro Grubisic was the council of the Republic of Croatia. But the person mentioned in the transcript, Ciro Ruzic, that person doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The transcript spells the name G-R-U-B-I-S-I-C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. It's at the bottom of page 156965. And it precedes the name Milan Kovac. It's spelled G-R-U-B-I-S-I-C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, yes. But on page 0156938, in the title you can see the name Ciro Ruzic. So I really don't know who was present. Was it either Ciro Ruzic or Ciro Grubisic. I've never heard of the person Ruzic -- Ruzic as a political figure in the political life in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kovac, if your saying that you don't recognise the name Ciro Ruzic, does that mean that that person doesn't exist? Why would you need to recognise all the persons who are present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading the names of people -- persons present, from President Tudjman, Minister Boban, and -- I know in the political life of the Croatia, I knew at least by surname the -- all the political figures who had -- and people who had important political roles there. And I had not heard of such a person, Ciro Ruzic. You can check through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs whether such a person exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I can't find that page that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I -- it's page -- Your Honours, it's -- I have it here. It's page 0156938. And I'm afraid it's not in the bundle, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How does the witness have it, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The witness has been given the complete transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So my apologies. But we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here as well. But Your Honours, I don't think that we should go into this, because really I asked the question about Grubisic and not about Ciro Ruzic, and I think the witness is trying to confuse things now. And it may well be a completely different person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's precisely -- this is the point. And when the Honoured Judge will read it -- Ciro Ruzic has a page and a half of his transcript, and he is represented as the deputy leader of the political activity in the HVO, the active administrator for the political department of HVO. And this is the -- would be the second person of the HVO and he has one and a half page of text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the last page, we have clearly the names of Ciro Grubisic and Milan Kovac. And this is from the entire transcript. We have not received the entire transcript, just certain pages of the transcript from the meeting in the Vila Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krzic, the issue here is not whether some other people were present at the meeting or not. Is the witness himself present at the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- Your Honours, I will not go into a discussion into this. The witness is saying that this is -- that the meeting probably wasn't even held and that the names have been made up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I've noticed the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, the statement made by the witness. But we'll read all the transcripts ourselves at a later stage. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, having read out this line just to you -- and your name being mentioned here, is it still your testimony that you were not present at this meeting in the villa of Dalmacija in Split on November 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not attend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's our submission that you were present at that meeting. And on the basis of that, I want to ask you some questions of this -- on this transcript. Let's move to the first page of this transcript. The very first page of the transcript. I don't know if the -- maybe the usher can organise the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How will a witness who asserts that he was not present, how can he answer questions despite the assertions of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you know there's argument between the Prosecution and the witness. One says that he was present there. The witness said he was not. So I believe that the Prosecution is going to show more evidence to prove to his own argument. It's a matter of the credibility of this witness, Mr. Krsnik. Yes, Mr. Bos, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Kovac, I'd like you to look at the first page of this transcript. This is when the president opens the meeting. And in the second paragraph of that -- of that first page, he says the following: "The problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the problem of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it's also a problem of the Croatian state and its future." And then a few lines down: "We have always kept in mind the strategic interests of importance for the future of the Croatian people and Croatia in general, including the questions of borders -- of its borders." Now, let me ask you, what do you think that President Tudjman meant that -- when he said that it's also a problem of the Croatian state and its future?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to surmise what President Tudjman was thinking. Yesterday I spoke, however, about the policy of HDZ, who was the president of the Republic, was also its president. And he said that as long as there's no stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there can be no stability or peace in Croatia, because Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina have very close ties, infrastructural ties, railroad, road networks. They have also -- Bosnia has an outlet to the coast at Neum. But President Tudjman never -- but never, be it in open or covertly, of the divisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina and later on annexation of parts of it to Croatia. But he insisted that the Croatian people living in Bosnia and Herzegovina irrespective of the numbers of Serbs and Bosniaks, must maintain its right to its language, its culture, its religion because the Croatian people have been living there for thousands of years. That was his fundamental thought. And the 1990 constitution also stipulates that Croatia will care for its people wherever they live. But that does not imply that it will interfere in the policy of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He insisted that it would be necessary -- that it's necessary to go to Sarajevo to cooperate with them, to avoid excesses, to avoid conflict. But if you pull out of the context certain events out of the general framework, they -- you are faced with a different situation. But if -- when Vukovar, Dubrovnik are being burnt -- are burning, when a million of people are coming, refugees are coming only with plastic bags, when there is no tourism, when we're threatened with a collapse, why would we go in for an additional conflict with a neighbouring country which would generate additional thousands upon thousands of refugees?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What do you think that President Tudjman meant when he said that he would keep in mind the strategic interests, including the questions of borders?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strategic interest of the Republic of Croatia, as I have said, are peace and that satisfied three nations [As interpreted] living in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the strategic interest of Croatia. As far as the borders are concerned, he insisted upon the inviolability of the republican borders, because what kind of a president would that be with one third of a country occupied, when Croats and non-Serbs were evicted from these areas, and when those who occupied parts of Croatia are demanding to create the greater Serbia at the expense of these Croatian territories? Do you really think that President Tudjman would seek to change borders in another country as an experienced historian and politician, he knew what it was all about. He demanded the independence of Croatia, of the Croatian Republic, and the maintenance of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina with all their rights and their sovereign rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Kovac, let's move on to the third page of this transcript. This is where President Tudjman refers to a secret agreement which he signed in Vienna that, and this was an agreement that President Tudjman signed together with President Izetbegovic. And the content of this agreement is described in the second paragraph of the -- page 3. Well, this is the English version. And for the B/C/S version, it's on page 0156866, which starts with the sentence "They have agreed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we'd be very happy with the Prosecutor would show us this secret agreement and give it to the witness, and then we'd be more than happy to discuss it, the one that Mr. Tudjman signed with Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think the first question asked by the Prosecution will be whether this witness know or not about this agreement. Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall President Tudjman discussing this secret agreement at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall it if I wasn't at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just see what President Tudjman says about this meeting. And I'm quoting now from page 3. "They --" and then it's referred to President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic -- "they have agreed that the relations between the Bosnian Muslim republic and the Republic of Croatia, within the union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, must develop in all areas with an aim to create a common state, which will subsequently enter into a confederal relationship with the Republic of Croatia." And then if we move down a few paragraphs, President Tudjman says the following: "With such an agreement, our aim has been to protect the strategic interest of the Croatian people in Bosnia. By not only obtaining Herceg-Bosna but also by entering into a close alliance with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts Muslims, in order to protect the interests of the Croatian people and the Croatian areas within the Muslim Republic." So again, my question: Do you recall President Tudjman talking about this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I repeat for the third time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. The witness has already answered, and that was my objection, that he has repeated several times that he had not been at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, both the Defence counsels have to trust your witness, because your witness could answer those questions. There's no need to stand up consistently and to interrupt the proceedings. I'm sorry, Witness. You may continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether I was present and heard President Tudjman. I said I wasn't present, and I do not know what they discussed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I just read out to you, wouldn't you agree that this shows direct involvement of the Republic of Croatia into the territorial division of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what you have just quoted, as President Tudjman's words after a year later, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded in confederation with Croatia. It was signed in Washington. This does not mean any division of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- is the internal organisation which was accepted by the International Community in Washington. The Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is made of Bosniak, Muslims, and Croats -- and Republika Srpska is the other entity. And this agreement was signed in Washington, which allowed to sign the -- an agreement on the confederation between the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. But that does not mean the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the sense that you are talking about, that it would then be annexed to the Republic of Croatia. The strategic interest of the Croatian state is for the Croats to remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they will stay only if they enjoy the same rights as the other two peoples. That was President Tudjman's idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But wasn't it President Tudjman's idea to create a great Croatia, a Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Never. Never did he ever mention it or does it -- or can you find it in any document. There was never any decision taken at any level of power about the change of the republic's borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on in the transcript. And I'd like you now to look at page -- for the B/C/S version, page 01566933 and 6934. For the English version, it's page 0182812. Now, Witness, at this meeting there were a lot of -- several high military HVO officials present at this meeting. General Slobodan Praljak was at that meeting. He was the HVO Commander-in-Chief. Do you know who he is? Do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Slobodan Praljak from before, from the -- as a film critic and an author, a writer. I believe he wrote some books. And I knew him later too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I've been asked whether -- if you could please not make any notes on the transcripts, because the -- because this is an original exhibit and we would like you not to write on that exhibit. Now, Witness, do you know a man by the name of Zarko Tole?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I know the gentleman. I met Mr. Zarko Tole. I think he's a general or colonel in the Croatian army. But I have met him. I've seen him in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His present function is a colonel in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't really know what he is now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you said that he was a colonel in the Croatian army, which time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of parliament. And as far as military matters are concerned, I am really not a qualified person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you were asked a very simple question. You are not an unintelligent man. You were asked: "When you said that this gentleman, Zarko Tole, was a general or a colonel in the Croat Croatian army, what period were you talking about?" It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the wartime, the '90s, the time of conflict, aggression against Croatia. I know that he took part in the defence of Croatia and I know that he returned from I don't know where. I don't know where he was born -- that he returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina. From that time I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, if you say the time of conflict, are you referring to the conflict between Croatia and the Serbs, in 1991? Or are you referring to the conflict between ... ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was an active-duty man right up to the Dayton Accords. I think so. But, of course, I have no way of knowing the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness, let me tell you that Mr. Zarko Tole, when he was present at this meeting, was there as an HVO -- in his representative as an HVO Chief of the Main Staff, so not representing Croatian army but representing the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm merely performing my duty as a counsel. And may I be objected. May we see in this transcript where does it say Zarko Tole? For some people there's both a first name and last name. For some, no. But Zarko Tole doesn't say anywhere. It only says Tole. Tole is a last name. A very common one. So how can the Prosecutor affirm that the -- that he's Zarko Tole? And I believe this objection is well grounded, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I don't think the question has something to do with this document at all, because the Prosecution is asking a question about a certain person, whether this person know that one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honours. The question is -- and you can find it on page -- look at the Prosecutor's question. [In English] "HVO chief in the main staff." So this meeting, the meeting of the -- the transcript of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Clark, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: He asked him first, "do you know Praljak?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And he explained. And the next question is, "do you Zarko Tole?" That's the question he was asking. We're really getting bogged down on detail. And you both are being overprotective of your witnesses since the Defence case started. None of the witnesses you have called so far are uneducated people. They're very high standing people in the Croatian community and yet you don't allow them to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but allow me to answer. I'm not behaving -- I'm not being overprotective, Your Honours. I'm merely discharging my duties as a counsel. Please, you have the transcript. The last Prosecutor's questions was that Zarko Tole was at this meeting. And he keeps asking this witness about this. And my question is: Where did the transcript say that it was Zarko Tole? Your Honours, surely I know what I'm talking about. [In English] Surely, yes. [Interpretation] And the third question was: "Zarko Tole at this meeting in this presidential transcript." And all I asked was where does it say Zarko Tole in this transcript. I'm really sorry, but I must do my duty. This is not the protective role or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... This document. Ask your question directly, Mr. Bos, whether this person knows that Mr. Tole, Zarko Tole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think I did ask this question, whether this person knows Mr. Zarko Tole, and he gave an answer. And my next step will be that I'm going take this witness to the transcript and let him see any statements that were made by Mr. Tole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this case, Mr. Bos, you have to establish which Tole it is. Is that Zarko Tole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's our position that the person who is referred to as Tole here is Zarko Tole, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, show us, you know, whether his full name appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I can't do that right now. I'd have to go through the transcript. And maybe we can stop now for a break and I can consult the transcript again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It is time for a break. We'll break here until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, during the break I went through the transcript, and it is correct. I couldn't find the first name of Tole in the transcript. But what I did find is that whenever this Tole was speaking, he's referred to the main staff on several occasions. And I can give you a few examples. This is on Registry -- yeah. I'm afraid I -- I don't know if the Court has the full English translation of the presidential transcripts at hand now, because I don't think it will all be included in the -- in the binder I provide. Anyway, there are a few examples. For example, Tole is talking about the responsibility of the main staff constituted to a large extend in gathering soldiers for the front line, former units, et cetera. "As for the work done by the main staff -- and I would only like to comment on it within the limits of my of competence -- I think it's not being put to adequate use." A bit further down, "the vanity, which leads to a situation where the relationship between those who need to work very closely together turns sour, down to the direct interference in the activity of the main staff, on the part of president of the municipalities and even further." And then on the part which is also included in the exhibit binder, which is page number 4: "The main staff is currently working on putting out the --" if I may use the expression, "competence individuals who would also participate in fighting for the tasks that were mentioned by the commander." So this Mr. Tole has been referring to the main staff on numerous occasions. And if I just made sure the Court and also the witness -- Exhibit P559.1. And I -- we've made some -- it's an existing Prosecution exhibit. And I have some copies here for everyone in the courtroom. And maybe we could also put a copy on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this is a request signed by Major General Slobodan Praljak and is addressed to -- to the Ministry of the Defence of the Republic of Croatia? It refers to the posting of HV -- officers in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understand what cross-examination is - but you will instruct me and correct me if I am wrong - we said that the Prosecutor and just the Defence in the examination-in-chief cannot -- may not misrepresent the facts. The Prosecutor has just said it was signed by Mr. Praljak, and here we have the name Martic. It is quite legible. It has nothing to do with the knowledge of the language. So why does it say somebody else signed it? Why say it was Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Bos will give us an explanation on the signature of this document on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know why it says Martic. Probably because Martic signed for Mr. Praljak. But I don't think that's the issue here. I think the issue is whether brigadier Zarko Tole was in fact Chief of the HVO Main Staff. That's what I'm trying to find out here and that's the issue here, not whether there's a different signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Witness, is it correct that this is a request whereby Mr. Zarko Tole, an HVO officer is requested to be at the disposal of the HVO general staff -- the chief of the HVO general staff? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Republic of Croatia, I was not a part of the military structure. I was a member of the parliament. And I go by the laws of the Republic of Croatia. This document which says "military secrets, strictly confidential," has -- was never in the diet of the Republic of Croatia or in the national security board where the -- where the confidentiality would be removed. And therefore, I cannot comment because I must abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Mr. Bos. I mean, he can't know anything about the document. All you can do is show it to him and he says, "I never saw it before," and we take the document for what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I agree, Your Honour. And -- but I -- you know, I had to do this because of a comment by counsel, my learned counsel, and not because of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then ask you this, Mr. Kovac: How much Toles would you know who would talk about the functioning of the main staff in November 1993 within the -- with the President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know who Mr. -- President Tudjman talked with. I know Zarko Tole from the media by and large, because he was a person who after the aggression against Croatia transferred from the Yugoslav People's Army to the Croatian army. And I know that he was captured for 15 months in Manjaca near Banja Luka. I really cannot remember what post brigadier or General Tole held, whether he was the head -- chief or what. I really cannot say for certain. But I say I cannot discuss document which is are marked "military secret, strictly confidential," because the Croatian diet has not removed this classification, has not declassified it. And I repeat, I do not know how these documents ended up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you to comment on some of the things that this Mr. Tole said at that meeting. And I'm now referring to -- I don't know if you still have the presidential transcript in front of you -- I'm referring to page 0156933.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I don't know if you could put that document in front of the witness. The English translation will be page 0182812.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat if number again, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it's the presidential transcript which is on the left side of him. And I need him to look at page 0156933.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Kovac? This is when Mr. Tole starts to talk. The third paragraph, which starts with "But without the help from the Croatian army." Do you have that? It may be on the next page. It reads the following: "But without the help from the Croatian army in what way and how, I think it will be very difficult from a military intelligence data -- for my military intelligence data say that the Muslims are at this moment targeting Mostar and Gornji Vakuf." This is Mr. Tole reporting to Mr. Tudjman. And a bit further down: "That is why I believe that during the planning and realisation stages, the Croatian Defence Council staff must be in direct consultation with the Croatian army staff in order to be able to estimate which forces, what, where, and what -- and at what time are to be used and how." Now, Mr. Kovac, wouldn't you agree that this last statement by the HVO chief of main staff assumes direct military involvement of the Croatian army in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am not protecting the witness -- far be it from me. But I'm trying to protect the fairness of this case. The witness has said almost two hours ago that he was not present -- that he had not been present at the meeting. And now if he's invited about something that somebody else thought, then it is inviting his speculation, and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this aspect, Mr. Bos, I agree with the Defence counsel. The witness said that he did not present at that meeting -- he knows next to nothing about this meeting. And how could you ask him to comment on a statement delivered at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, one of the reasons why I'm asking him to comment is because it's our position that he was at that meeting. And I want to cross-examine this witness on that assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have -- do you have some -- some other evidence to show that this witness was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No. I've shown you the evidence which I've referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. You have just said what I was about to say when I stood up to object to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts this frequent claim of the Prosecution that Milan Kovac was present at the meeting. He should be shown some evidence to this effect. Besides, the Prosecutor has not shown any order of this Chamber or this Tribunal regarding this evidence nor the correspondence between the Prosecutor's office and the relevant authority, be it the president Stipe Mesic or the office for cooperation with this Tribunal, so we could really see in this which way was this documentation handed over to the Prosecutor's office. It would be fair to show this to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, we have to be fair to this witness. If he denied that he was not at that meeting [As interpreted], how could I ask him to comment on the document you were showing to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, again -- I mean, it's our submission that he was present at that meeting. And I think we've shown sufficient evidence to that effect by showing that page on the transcript where he's been referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. Bos. I think we were waiting here eagerly to see if you would produce evidence to discredit this witness in relation to his evidence about being present at the meeting. And so far you have only referred to what other people have said. We must be fair. We were waiting for you to say that there was some other evidence to show. But, perhaps you'd ask this witness whether he was in Split at the particular time. And that might explain the reference to him being present here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard the question of the Judge. Were you in Split in November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recollect, I wasn't there, but I'm sure I wasn't at the meeting. But where exactly was I at the time, I would have to check my notes in order to see where I was as a deputy. If I had been at this meeting, I would certainly comment every sentence. However, I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, what I actually would have liked Mr. Bos to ask you -- so I'll ask you it myself -- is that is it possible that you were definitely not at the meeting, but that you may have been with the presidential entourage in Split at that time and that is -- that would explain why the late president Tudjman would refer to two men being present here. Might have been present in Split but not necessarily at the meeting. I was just wondering if that was an explanation. Let him answer first, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat: In no uncertain term that is I did not attend that meeting, and as I'm under oath, I will not be able to assert a hundred per cent whether I was in Zagreb, in Osijek, or in Split at the time. However, had I been on that day in Split, I would probably -- probably -- have been attending that meeting. And this is just a confirmation for me that I wasn't even in Split. That would be one of the arguments speaking in favour of this assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was it normal, Mr. Kovac -- was it normal for the president to attend meetings in Split? Was he frequently there -- the late president, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he often went to Dalmatia, to Split, to Sadar [phoen], Dubrovnik. I cannot remember all of his visits there. But throughout the war he would often frequently visit Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And is it the situation, Mr. Kovac, that as part of the -- the government at the time and as adviser to the president on, I think you told us, privatisation of state property -- as adviser that you would attend many meetings with the president, or was it unusual for you to be present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the Minister for Privatisation in 1997 and 1998, Minister for Privatisation. But I was never an adviser to the president. And from 1993, I was exclusively and only a deputy in the Croatian diet, in the parliament. And it wouldn't be usual for the president to invite the deputies to attend such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So can we take it, Mr. Kovac, that your position in vis-a-vis President Tudjman would make it unusual for you to be present at my meeting, in Split or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be unusual for me in my capacity as a deputy of the diet to be invited to attend such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clarified the situation for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Chamber, Judge Clark, that what is in the transcript that it is President Tudjman who said that Mr. Kovac and the other person is present in the transcript. It doesn't say who stated that. This is all I wish to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Bos, could I ask you to withdraw your question concerning this presidential transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. I won't belabour this issue any longer, Your Honours. But I'm just curious, because the witness in answering the questions of Judge Clark -- the witness in the beginning said that if he would have been in Split, he probably would have attended that meeting. That's how he started off with his testimony. And I -- and then later on he says completely the opposite. And I'm just wanting to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you have some questions concerning on this point, you may ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, that -- that would be my question, Mr. Kovac. Why did you say that if you would have been in Split at the time you probably would have attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that -- I don't think I said that if I were in Split that I'd be attending the meeting. I don't think I said it. Probably it is an error. I explained that -- how the president would invite persons to a meeting. It's not that if one were present in that city that one would go and have a meeting with the president. Because, Your Honour, it's my first time in a courtroom in any of my function. I've never been either a witness or as a prosecutor or as a counsel. For me, maybe I have a bit of a difficulty to find my bearings. But I didn't -- what I said, that if I were in Split that I'd probably be at the meeting -- no, that wouldn't be like that. It would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll rest the issue, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, don't worry if you're nervous, because you're not the only one. Every witness feels exactly the same way, and you're doing very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I have just a few more questions, Mr. Kovac. As a member of parliament, do you know a man by the name of Branko Barbic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what -- what is his function -- or what was his function in 1992? Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was his function at -- in 1992. But at present he is the secretary of the committee which I'm heading in the parliament, the committee for immigration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Branko Barbic also work in -- have a function in parliament in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. Probably he was working in some administration. He had an administrative post. But maybe I could ask him tomorrow when I return to my post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, if I -- if I tell you that Mr. Barbic in 1992 was the military attache for the troops in Central Bosnia and Southern Bosnia, taking care of supplies for the troops in these places, would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was possible. He was working employed in the administration of the Croatian parliament, of the diet. And I don't think that he could have been at the same time occupying the post of attache for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts Central Bosnia that or whatever you've said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, witness, what would you say if I say that we had a witness in this courtroom who claimed that he -- who actually was a mercenary in Bosnia-Herzegovina and he claimed that he was recruited after an interview in the office of Mr. Branko Barbic in the parliament building in Zagreb? What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call -- invite Branko Barbic to come here and say what that is all about, to clarify -- to clarify on these matters, if it is the truth, of course. I doubt it. It's the first time I hear something like that for this secretary, the secretary of the committee that I'm heading today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Finally, Witness, is it correct that you have always felt a close affiliation for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a Croat from Bosnia and Herzegovina, I did have a particular feeling for the Croatian people there. It is their where my mother of 80 years lives there today, as well as my two brothers with their families, and I am visiting them regularly every month. And as the president of the committee for immigration, I on a daily basis receive tens and tens of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats who have been banished from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the Republika Srpska. I have to care for them. I assist them to see that they survive up to the moment when they will be able to return home. And that is the care, and these are the feelings that I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in Posusje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a village about north-west of Siroki Brijeg, is that correct, in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from Siroki Brijeg are always offended if we say we live from the -- to the west from them. It is -- we are distant some 30 kilometres from Siroki Brijeg and some 5 kilometres from the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two more questions. Witness, did you on the 7th of July, 1997, did you attend the funeral of Mr. Mate Boban as an official delegate for the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't an official delegate. I went in my personal capacity, as a private person, to attend the funeral of Mate Boban whom I had known since our school days. Later, Mate Boban was a director of a company with which my firm cooperated up till 1990. So I was there in my personal capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. Kovac, sit also correct that you attended an art auction in Siroki Brijeg on the 29th of January, 1999, of which the entire proceedings was for the benefit of the families of the Bosnian Croats who were accused by this Tribunal at that time, like Mr. Blaskic, Mr. Kordic, Aleksovsky? Is it correct that you attended that auction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to recall and try to remember. I attended many an auction throughout Croatia for humanitarian purposes. Also in Bosnia and Herzegovina I visited Posusje practically every month. And remember I attended that auction -- yes, I was there. It was some 20 kilometres from Posusje, where the auction was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you buy anything at that auction? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't buy anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I'll be very short. Re-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovac, how does one enter the building of the diet, the Croatian parliament? As a visitor, what is the procedure for entering the premises?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, why did you ask this question? Because this question was not mentioned in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was the witness who testified here, that was a mercenary, Allan Knudsen who said that he went into the parliament. I checked and I received data. I received a written paper that that person never entered the building of the parliament. And I just wanted to avail myself of the fact that this witness is here and particularly because a question was raised in connection with Mr. Barbic and is connected with this testimony. And maybe this will be the last occasion for having a description of how one can enter the building. That person, that witness, also stated that he had lunch with Mr. Barbic in the premises of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you kindly explain what is the procedure for entering.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in all other parliaments, you first must announce yourself. You must say whom you are visiting, present an identity card or a passport, and pass through the metal detector machine in case somebody comes with weapons, and the number of the identity card or the passport is written down, and only the person can go -- and visit only the person for which he states. And such a person escorted to the person he'll be visiting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This witness which was mentioned by the Prosecutor, he stated that he even had lunch in the parliament building. What will you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visitors do not have access to the restaurant for the deputies, and only official delegations can have access to that area also -- parliamentary delegations and others, either from the country or abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness -- the witness Allan Knudsen said he came as a mercenary, came to Croatia, and tried to find where he should go -- to which battlefield he should go. As such he came to the reception of the parliament, went to Mr. Barbic's office, had lunch with him, and he then sent him to the front -- to a certain front. What will you say to that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I were a volunteer, I'd go to the military staff. The parliament had nothing to do with it, particularly not the employees of the parliament. And they certainly cannot deploy anybody anywhere. This seems a bit strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked and I also received from -- an answer from the security service of the state parliament, and I received in the answer that such a person never entered that parliament. But let's leave this topic and pass on to another subject, very briefly. Do you know for how long Mr. Mesic was in the HDZ and what happened to his political career, and what functions he held, as far as your knowledge is concerned? And I'm referring to the period from 1990 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known Mr. Mesic since 1989, and together we were -- went together to -- and founded HDZ branches and chapters in Slavonia, the area that he is originally from. He was the first government president in 1990. Later he was elected in the diet as a member of the Croatian state for the Yugoslav presidency. After that he was the president of the diet, the speaker, up till 1994. And up till then, he was also a member of HDZ. After that he left the party and he founded a new party, the Croatian Independent Democrats, I believe was the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what month of 1994 did he leave HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the month of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up till April 1994, he was an active member of HDZ, and he participated in all its deliberations and in the shaping of the positions of it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was by his function the second person. He was, you know, the president of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it seems to me that you're coming to new ground, new issue of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In the cross, President Mesic was being raised constantly. This is a subject which I'm now doing in the redirecting. I wanted to know whether the witness knew that the -- the witness knows that Mr. Mesic was also settling personal accounts with other people in the HDZ. This is what I wanted to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: He's giving evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You -- well, Mr. Krsnik, you know the re-examination should be strictly confined in the cross-examination; otherwise the Prosecutor will have another opportunity to cross-examination on this subject. I believe that this issue has little to do with the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the cross lasted two hours. Of that, one and a half hour devoted to Mr. Mesic and the presidential transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have at least the right to ask the question whether the witness knows why the debate in the parliament, why all these laws and why did all this happen? Does he personally know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You should ask this question in your direct examination rather than in the re-examination, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if that is the case, we will have other opportunities with other witnesses to clarify this issue. I have no other questions, and I thank the witness for coming here and for highlighting and clarifying certain facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Any questions from judges? Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions, Mr. Kovac, in addition to the ones I asked during the trial. As you were one of the founding members of the HDZ, which you told us was the first real opposition party in the emerging Croatia -- it wasn't yet an independent country, can you tell me was the platform of the HDZ to be involved and concerned with Croats who lived in Herzegovina and parts of Bosnia? I'm not talking about Croats in Australia or Switzerland or Canada. I'm talking about people of Croatian ethnicity in Herzegovina and the parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that adjoined Croatia. I know it's a long question. What I'm basically saying is, was it the HDZ platform to be concerned with those people particularly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The platform of the HDZ was that under those conditions when Yugoslavia still existed, that in all the republics a multi-party system be ensured, the founding of parliamentary parties be enabled, and HDZ was founded in the Republic of Croatia with its chapters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I don't want you to tell me all about the platform of the HDZ. It's a specific question. Was it included as a tenant of the HDZ -- that -- and then the question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, those were not the goals of HDZ, to deal and focus on Croats -- people of Croat ethnicity in Herzegovina, in Bosnia -- in parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina had also been founded -- with its president, with its assembly, secretariat, its central board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. You have mentioned on a number of occasions and indeed many other witnesses from Croatia have told this Trial Chamber the same thing, that the constitution as opposed to the platform of the HDZ or indeed to the constitution of the HDZ, but the constitution of Croatia imposed a duty on the government of Croatia to care for the Croatian citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And what I wanted to know is that borrowed from your platform, the HDZ -- and clearly, if it wasn't part of the platform, then it couldn't have been. Perhaps you can explain to me the reasoning behind such an unusual inclusion in a constitution of a country, to be concerned with the citizens of another sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
