utterances.text: I think we were talking at cross-purposes and my -- please receive my apologies. The HDZ's platform treats equally Croats wherever they may be outside the Republic of Croatia. What I said, that unlike others, he did not treat in any specific way Croats in Herzegovina. It is the care for Croats wherever they might live outside Croatia. The constitution -- which article was it -- I believe 10th speaks of the concern -- the care for the Republic of Croatia for Croats outside Croatia, and it was taken from the HDZ's platform, but not only this small group of people in Herzegovina or in western part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just want you to be clear about, because I haven't -- I don't believe anybody has produced the constitution of Croatia for us to examine this. But I may be wrong about that. I couldn't find it myself, and I'm curious. Are you saying, Mr. Kovac, that the constitution does not specifically mention the Croats of Herzegovina or Bosnia and Herzegovina, just Croats outside the state boundaries in general? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats in general, living outside the borders of the Republic of Croatia. But the constitution does not define a special treatment towards individual states. I mean, it does not specify states by their name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So when witnesses have told this Trial Chamber that there was a duty and an obligation on the part of the government of Croatia to be concerned about the citizens, the Croatian -- the Croat citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they were legally incorrect? Is that what you're saying? Strictly speaking, they were incorrect. It was a general duty and not a specific duty.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a general obligation, an all-round obligation of the Republic of Croatia. It does not specify measures and in which way the Republic of Croatia will help them. But it is an obligation of the Republic of Croatia to take care of the Croats outside the Republic of Croatia. And it also embraces Croats in Herzegovina, as a sovereign constituent people which -- who also have the Croatian nationality, because we have not yet regulated with Bosnia-Herzegovina the issue of dual nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I want to be very specific, Mr. Kovac. And maybe you're uncomfortable in answering this. In the days when the Croatian constitution was passed, there was no conflict between Croatia and the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no attack of -- of Sarajevo or any of the problems that happened with the government being considered effective or otherwise. So it may be we're jumping the gun when we're talking about offering nationality. But what I want you to tell me is does the constitution mention in any place the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really do not know the constitution by heart. So I cannot say whether it mentions Bosnia-Herzegovina or not. But I do not think that it mentions any state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. Do you know why -- and again, you may not be the appropriate person to say. But as you were a founding member of the HDZ and you were obviously involved in every election that has taken place and maybe you were involved in the aspirations which formed part of the written constitution, do you know why the constitution of Croatia imposes an aspiration to protect Croats in Australia or Canada? Why was that done, and how could it be effected?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think the constitution says to protect the Croats outside the borders but, rather, that Croatia cares for and supports and helps the Croat people outside the Republic of Croatia. I think it was taken over. I think one can find it in other constitutions too. I do not have it. I believe that the Prosecutor's office will supply the translation of the constitution and the articles that refer to this subject, and then we shall know exactly what it says, because in the Croatian language it is "Skrb," which means care, it will take care of the Croat people outside its boarders. I do not know whether the counsel has the constitution, because Croats lived in Vojvodina, in Kosovo. And as early as 1990, when this constitution was promulgated, the Croats in Kosovo were already so -- in such danger that Croatia undertook all it could to help them, to save them. And we remember well with the help of the International Community when the last of them were evacuated from Janjevo. I believe that is the name of the place because there was a danger of the occupation by the Serb forces in Kosovo. Then in Vojvodina, in the Republic of Serbia there is a Croat enclave and they have been moving out all these years and coming to Croatia, so that across Yugoslavia -- not only Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mean, the Croatian people lived across Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So, do you think therefore that it was included there because the country recognised that the former Yugoslavia had many diverse pockets of effect groups and it was best to protect these pockets as best you could?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that, among other things too, because the constitution was promulgated in December 1990. And in August 1990 Serb -- Serbs had already blocked -- I don't know whether the Court is aware of that -- roads -- I don't know whether you realise that there was already the Serb insurgence in Croatia and we could already see what was happening in other republics. So this constitution reflected this state of affair then and which anticipated things that happened later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It makes more sense to me when I see it in that context. But if we move on -- you stated earlier on in your evidence that Croatia never declared war on -- on Bosnia and Herzegovina and vice versa and that during the entire conflict, there was -- there were diplomatic relations between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Two questions arising out of that: Did Croatia ever declare war on Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Croatia never declared war on Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you maintain a diplomatic presence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no diplomatic -- there was no diplomatic presence during that time, and there were no diplomats present in Belgrade in 1991. It was later on after 1993 -- 1992 or 1993. It was the first time that Croatia sent its ambassador to Belgrade. I do not know the exact date, but during the aggression there were no diplomatic relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did your country, to your knowledge, Croatia, send diplomatic representation to the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia had its consulate in Mostar. It had its consulate in Tuzla, in Bihac, in Banja Luka too later on, and its embassy in Sarajevo. As far as I know, those were the only offices responsible for the reception of delegations and missions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were also parliamentary delegations and some ministries, especially after the Washington Agreement, and afterwards the agreement on special relations. And I personally visited Sarajevo not less than ten times during that one year discussing -- agreeing -- negotiating about those special relations between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you -- I don't know if this is a word that you're used to or a concept or anything, but we've heard frequently testimony and references to the word "Banovina," and we've seen maps. In your platform as the HDZ, did the Banovina play any part?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Never. Platform or programme or declarations, no, that word was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You also mentioned and you gave testimony -- I fortunately the document wasn't translated -- about a cross-party parliamentary commission to Herzegovina to investigate, insofar as you could, why -- why there seemed to be mounting tension between the Croats and the Muslims. I think you said that you couldn't go to parts of Bosnia per se because in parts of Bosnia there was a raging conflict and it wasn't safe. But in Herzegovina, as a separate province I'm talking about, what did you find when you were there? What did you find as the reasons for the mounting tensions between the two communities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of that delegation. There were some other MPs, as I have said, all of the parliamentary parties were represented on it. And pursuant to the diet's decision, they were to visit all those towns, places, enclaves where conflicts had taken place between Croats and Muslims or conflicts might happen. But as I have said, through the international forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina and with the concierge [As interpreted] of the Sarajevo ambassador to Zagreb, they were given the guarantees that they would be able to visit all those places. But when they reached Medjugorje, that they -- and I believe it was the 1st of May -- that they had a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kovac. You see, I understood you -- I wouldn't ask you this question except that I understood you to say that you had actually visited Mostar at the beginning of May 1993. And you gave us a list of towns: Jablanica, Kiseljak, Zenica, all those. You personally didn't go to those places. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. I didn't. I gave you the names of all the members of the diet who did go. I gave their names. And two of them are still members of parliament. They were in it today -- Mr. Drago Krpina of the HDZ and Mr. Mato Arlovic of the SDP, social democratic party, who is today the vice-president of the diet. They are selective politicians to the diet. And three other members, I don't know what they do. But these two are like -- me being a member of the diet all the time. And it was said that the Defence would translate their conclusions and would file them then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I was only asking you all those questions because I thought you had been on the mission and wondered why even though the document wasn't translated you weren't telling us anything about it. But then obviously I missed the fact that you weren't there. I think any other questions that I would ask you in relation to the presidential transcripts would get us into very deep water, hot deep water, so we'll stay away from that. Thank you very much, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's question? Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I do not have any questions. I merely wish to notify the Chamber that the document was not translated because we had no time you know the trouble we're in with translators. But it will be translated and the same goes for the Croatian constitution and all the other documents. This is now our ninth or tenth witness -- I don't know. But we shall be translating them and tendering them with witnesses. The Defence will provide the truth, whatever it may be to this Honourable Court, and that is what we shall do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. We all wish you good luck in future. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It was a pleasure to be here, even though it was my first time. But I will remember these two days forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any documents to tender at this stage? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. These are Exhibits -- let me just ask the registrar, our Honourable and distinguished Madam Registrar which numbers shall we be using? The new ones? Because D1301, 302, 303.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: ID D1/305 has not been translated, so -- you know that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1/328, D1/329, D1/301, D1/302, and D1/323 were all tendered under Milan Kovac on the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, how about D1/303?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, you didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. D1/303, also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't have any objections to the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Except for the document of which there was no English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think those documents are admitted into the evidence except for document D1/305, which was not translated. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have only -- the Prosecution only have three exhibits to tender, which are P876.01, P876.02, and P876.03, which are the press articles which I used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, are they translated into the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but they are in English, which is a working language of this Tribunal. And I don't think we -- it's required to have them translated into B/C/S to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you know the problem is, Mr. Bos, those documents are media, you know, coverage, which in our view has very little probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going -- I won't discuss the probative value. But this is simply the question of whether they can be admitted. And it's my submission that press articles can also be admitted as exhibits and that we have many other press articles admitted as evidence in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have objections. The same one that the Prosecutor raised when I tried to tender some newspaper articles. I merely wish to remind Your Honours these articles should also be translated. That was your ruling, it was your order. But because of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts the poor probative value of these articles, we object to their admission, because you know the Defence has not produced a single newspaper article and sought its submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... We have to reserve our decision concerning the admission of these documents at a later stage, because certainly we have different views among the admission of those documents. Well, Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And shall we break first and then we'll come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at twenty minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. In view of the fact that you spoke -- your English is better than Croatian, I will question you in Croatian, and you please feel free to answer in English. I will give you instructions. You can see the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the text.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please answer -- begin your answer only when the dot is there and when it stops. And I also ask you to speak slowly. I've noticed that you speak very fast and interpreters will have problems in translating you into Croatian. So let us begin. As with every witness, I would like to ask you to present yourself to the Court, to present your curriculum up till 1990, and from 1990 till the present day. Please tell us -- indicate briefly what your positions and functions were which you performed.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I was -- [In English] In English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Whatever language we use, it has to be at half the speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the Canadian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's far too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Too fast. The first unit was the 44th field squadron of the Royal Canadian Engineers. The second unit was the infantry regiment, the 2nd PPCLI. And the third unit was the Royal Edmonton Regiment, which I left in about -- in 1982. I then worked for the correctional department in the province of Alberta, Canada. I was commander of the -- of the tactical team. I joined the French foreign legion in 1989. And after we were -- which is the Duzmati [phoen], the 2nd -- 2nd Infantry Regiment stationed in Nimes. And after the regiment returned from the Gulf, I returned to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, where were you born? What nationality are you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I was born in Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And what's your name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm coming to this. Zeljko Glasnovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Krsnik, in the -- the last few witnesses we've had to wait to find out. Why don't your witnesses -- why don't you say "please state your name," which is the very first thing one should do. Please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did, but the witness accelerated with everything he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I do know that you're here for the first time. Probably there's a bit of excitement. You're listening to the Croatian translations -- interpretation. You'll see the problems the interpreters have. And try to slow down your English. You have to bear in mind that also there's French interpretation. How old were you when you left for Canada? After that, you've been living -- throughout your life in Canada.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How old was he when we went to Canada? It was so fast the interpreters didn't pick it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was eight. Eight years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please slow down a bit. Please. And calmly. Tell us, did you receive any merits, recognition for the services you've rendered to the military in Canada and France?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please wait for the end of the question before he starts answering, because he overlaps with interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, it will be very hard work. Mr. Glasovic, if you don't calm down. Look at the computer - the dot. Listen to the Croatian interpretation coming to you through the earphones. Everything depends on the interpretation. Nobody can follow us if our questions and answers overlap. Therefore I ask you once again to concentrate, to focus on the computer or the earphones. My last questions was did you receive any medals for the services you rendered in the Canadian army, the French army, the Gulf, and which medals were these?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I had medals -- actually decorations in the Canadian army. Not medals, but decorations. And I had two medals in the French army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive decorations or medals in the Gulf war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I will ask you slowly, since you have returned to Croatia when did you come to Croatia and describe all your positions, slowly, up till the present day. But slowly.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I came to Croatia at the end of July 1991. I joined the Zrinski Battalion, which was a regular -- or -- a regular formation of the Croatian army. I fought on several fronts. Actually, a better word, I think is -- I fought in several regions. And when the war in Croatia ended in January 1992, I left the Croatian army and went to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you come to Bosnia and Herzegovina and what duties did --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... First were to go to either -- either Bihac or Orasje in the Posavina area. But I ended up in Tomislavgrad, because -- like, the majority -- the majority of my -- the members of my platoon were from the Tomislavgrad area or Western Herzegovina. My first function there was organising the Tomislavgrad defence force. And that was in January of 1992. I was wounded in April, and I returned in the seventh month of 1992, where I was first 2IC of the Tomislavgrad Brigade -- I was second in command of the Tomislavgrad Brigade in July of 1992. I became commander in the fall of 1992, and I stayed commander till end of 1993. In 1994, I took over as commander of the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, in short.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1994, I left the Guards Brigade and led three tactical groups of the HVO. There's a mistake here. In the summer of 1995, I should say, I left. And I stayed commander of the three tactical groups till the end of hostilities in November of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue with your professional career in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Still the HVO. There was no such federation army. In 1996, I was appointed as a programme manager for the MPRI programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would you -- would you explain what MPRI is and explain it to the Honourable Counsel?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Was the train and equip programme, sponsored by the United States State Department, to train and equip the Federation army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you in the federal army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In 1997, I became commander of the 1st Croatian Guards Corps. In 1998, I became the commander of Trade Doc. Trade Doc -- trading and doctrine command, which is a training and doctrine command of the newly formed Federation army. I stayed in that position until 1999. In the year -- last year, I was appointed as the military adviser to the Minister of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I held that position till April -- April 4th of this year, when I resigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your rank?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Federation army.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the transcript, your answers are not entered in the transcript because you are speaking too fast. I have to draw your attention to that -- too fast. Maybe the best would be if you look at me. And when I give you a nod, then you may proceed with your answer. Maybe that would be the best way.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever is more efficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript, your rank has not been entered.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Three star general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question to you would be: Do you -- did you go to Bosnia and Herzegovina in capacity as a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I was a volunteer, like many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us then this -- -- you said you were born in Zagreb. And what are your roots? Where are your parents from?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: My grandparents are originally -- they're from Bosnia and Herzegovina. My grandfather is from Bihac and my grandmother from Orasje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any live relatives even today in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Could you repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we're still not getting your answer. Would you please answer it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have relatives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us -- [In English] Or you have a question maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It might be easier all round if the witness read the screen rather than looking at you, because I think -- I think that but I'm not sure that it's in English there. Is it? Even for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. I think the channel the witness uses should be English one so that he could know whether it has been translated into English or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, everything you're saying is then reproduced on the screen. You can follow on the screen. You can see when I shall complete my question. Only then you can begin answering that question. Mr. Glasnovic, could you tell us what was the situation in the HVO when you arrived to Tomislavgrad. And if you could describe to the Chamber what the situation was and circumstances were in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions in one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the first question, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: In -- when I came there, the HVO did not exist. And for the second part, the HVO was an army that was not formed in a traditional manner that normal armies are formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was precisely for that reason on the basis of your experience, the experience you've had, you can assist this Chamber and qualify the level of military organisation in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: In the outset, the HVO was not a trained and ready force. It was built up in phases from 1992 till 1995. There was no -- there was no standardised tactical doctrine. There were no trained -- there was no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts trained cadre, very few trained officers. Tactical sustainment was at the municipal level, and was not successfully centralised till the end of the war. As I said, leadership was the biggest problem, combined with a lack of equipment. And that is basically the answer that I would give.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned leadership, to which leadership were you referring when you said that this was a problem?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to military leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain the reason to this Chamber why was that so.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I think there's a slight mistake in my answer. It should say I was referring, not preferring to military leadership. An army is an organisation that enables leadership and initiative from the highest to the lowest levels of command. Basic training which turns a civilian into a soldier lasts a minimum of four months specialised training -- specialised training, for example, advanced infantry training, lasts about six months. So it's obvious we didn't have the luxury nor the time nor the equipment to train our people properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the case also of military commanders? And if they existed -- and who were they in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: In the outset, the commanders were basically patriots who returned home to defend their villages and towns because the scenario that unfolded in Croatia previously was going to unfold in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All the indicators were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall come to that perhaps later. Now I'd like to know at the outset you said that they were the commanders. And later on how did one become a commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly through intestinal fortitude, through initiative and talent for leadership. It was positive selection under fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any ranks in the HVO in 1992, 1993, or rather, how was the command structured? The first question is: "Were there any ranks in the army?"

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: There were no ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were they introduced for the first time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: The ranks were formally worn in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about this commander -- this rankless command? How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: There were job descriptions -- or I should say -- I have to say this in Croatian. [Interpretation] Formation posts. [In English] I think a more appropriate term is a posting corresponding to the job description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the troops call those people who held those posts?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of them were just from the same municipality, from the same town, or the same village. So they were on a first name basis mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that they also addressed them as commander from the lowest ranking unit. Can you explain which was the lowest -- the smallest unit, which was the largest unit, in an army as organised as you described it and whether they addressed them as commanders, from this lowest ranking to the highest ranking unit? Or how? You are an expert. Will you please help us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not too sure if I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these soldiers -- how were they organised? Let's have this as the first question. How were the units organised from the smallest one to the largest one?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, even in the outset, again, the defence of the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was based on the Territorial Defence force. But this also fell apart, this system, in 1990 because the Serbian army -- or actually, the Yugoslav JNA, the Yugoslav army, so-called, was Serbianised and the weapons were taken away from the Territorial Defence forces in the Croat and Muslim components -- or in the Croat and Muslim territories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Never mind. I do not want to lead you. But did -- was -- what was called the smallest unit? Was it a platoon? Was the largest one a brigade, or what? In 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: You see, that's a difficult question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Because each municipality feel that its own troops -- excuse me. I think -- there's another mistake here in the translation. Field -- -- not -- not feel, but -- be fielded. I can speak for my own for the Tomislavgrad area. I started -- I started with a wing force platoon. I'm sorry. Reinforced. The next step was a battalion, which was difficult to form because its leadership was Serbian and -- and the military occupation on specialties within the battalion were posted elsewhere in the previous JNA structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the name of the man who led this reinforced platoon? What -- how did the soldiers address him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: "Svabo."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you mean your -- Tomislavgrad. Uh-huh. But did they address him as commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Everyone knew each other. As I said, it was -- it was informal. Nobody called me commander, for example. They called me "Glava," which literally means "head."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are also the first four letters in your last name, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was because of -- it was because I addressed each soldier as "head."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Tell me, before I ask you something else, can you tell us what was the ratio of professionally trained soldiers and volunteers in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I think I'm -- now I'm hearing French translation on the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The English -- we're still getting French translation on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you've forgotten my last question, you can read it in the transcript. So what was the ratio -- or was there any -- between the professionally trained soldiers and volunteers? Or how many soldier professionals there were and how many volunteers were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Generally, the majority of the soldiers were volunteers. There was -- there was a sprinkling of ex-JNA officers and those that served in other western armies. The ratio is hard to define.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulties with discipline, and how did you put in order this volunteer army, if I might call it that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I basically had a mission. And the mission was to defend Tomislavgrad and its municipality. So obviously, I asserted my authority and the coordination between my co-workers in the unit and the civilian authorities was always correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Glasnovic, I asked you all these questions so that the Honourable Court could hear it from the man who participated in all that, because the Prosecution claims that the HVO was an army which was organised, well, almost as NATO, and that they were even punished when they failed to clean their rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no quarrel with the witness. And I apologise for interrupting. Counsel, that's -- Your Honour, that's not correct. That's never been our position. We've never taken that. It's not fair for counsel to characterise it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, of course, Your Honours. But God has given me a good and long memory. The cross-examination of Mr. Praljak, the Prosecutor said verbatim, "it was such a well disciplined army, as he knows from previous case, that they were punished even when they failed to clean their rifles." That was the position during the cross-examination of General Praljak. And I can repeat every word, word for word. So that I asked if indeed that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection stands. It's still an incorrect statement of the Prosecution's position. We objected to it very much. He can simply put questions to the witness and get answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: For one thing, there was no infrastructure in the municipalities where these units were stationed originally to house, feed, drill, or properly train a large number of troops. We used, for example, in the outset, again, schools for housing trainees. Any military man knows the infrastructure needed to train in one platoon, not to mention the leadership needed and the expertise. You need so many square metres per man to sleep. For a battalion, how many washrooms do you need? You need ranges built to zero your weapons. You have to train all levels of command and not just the lowest level. We had no staff and command college. We had no trained and ready NCO corps. It takes decades to train and build a non-commission officer, a senior non-com. I'll just underline what I said before. In 1992 there was no trained and ready force in -- in Western Herzegovina, or anywhere else for that matter, I think, where Croats and Muslims were majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Glasnovic, if you've finished. Did these volunteers want to go elsewhere and defend other places, or were they willing only to defend their village, their town? Where did they sleep and how did you call them up for an action?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the majority of these volunteers went to the villages and towns where they were born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulties when sending them to front lines away from their villages or towns?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously everyone had a problem because, basically, they were housed in their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber -- and I will show you the exhibit D1/82. Before I show it to you, can you tell us in a nutshell what was the command system like in the HVO in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please, if you can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please describe it in your own words, and then we shall move on to the chart.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this diagram, first of all, this structure you're showing me here -- structure, meaning force structure. Not structure as building, but force structure -- did not exist in 1992 at the beginning of hostilities. It started to crystalise in late 1992, and somewhat jelled as a cohesive unit somewhere towards the end of 1993. It's self-explanatory. You have your -- your civilian commander, which I presume Mr. Krsnik, would be the president; your Ministry of Defence, with its sectors; your headquarters, your army headquarters with -- I presume it's five -- I presume were four sectors -- personnel, military intelligence, operations, and logistics -- and unit attached directly under the command of that military headquarters. Below we have four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for interrupting. I've been listening to the witness's testimony very carefully for the last few moments. I don't know if he's commenting on the chart and saying this is what in fact it was. But he's stated several of his answers "I would presume," and I would like to know the difference whether he's just making -- assuming and presumptions. I'm not questioning his credibility. But what whether what he's telling us -- or whether he's saying what on this chart is in fact the HVO structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. If using this chart, we must concentrate on that. And do you have a English version of that chart, Mr. Krsnik? If you have, would you please put the English version on the ELMO so that everybody could know what is it about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, Your Honour, I understand the chart here. I don't think I need an English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The problem is to let us to us to understand this chart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour. But [Interpretation] But whether the -- and it was due to the help of the Prosecution, because translated it. If you will remember, they used it during Mr. Praljak. I mean, if it will help, this one has some added writing, some added text -- but if we could use this one. I have it. Yes, never mind. We can use it. But whatever was -- whatever comments there are in writing here do not mean much. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between French and English transcripts

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: This is basically the chart -- I say basically, and I assume because I'm not -- I don't know the structure of the Ministry of Defence or the -- or the presidential structure in 1992 or 1993. I was -- I was then at the level of -- brigade level. But this is basically the HVO structure from fall of 1992, till the fall of 1993 -- or the winter of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point -- could you tell us where were you in this whole structure.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I was in OZ Tomislavgrad, which is a brigade in that zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see here these blue boxes, and we see how lines go in their direction. And then it says "special purpose units" and "professional units." What can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Those units were an asset, my understanding. Because command relationships were not clear and cut. I have to underline that -- that fact. Is that these units were assets commanded by either the Ministry of Defence or the headquarters of the HVO -- the headquarters pictured here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard here a great deal about something which is called ATG. What is it? What is an ATG in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: It could be a misnomer. To me it's a misnomer. These units -- I had no such units in my sector of operations or in my unit in the brigade. But my understanding is that they were small units used for intervention or front -- on critical -- for critical tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that -- would they be units for special purposes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Again I say -- I had no such units in my sector. I had -- I had platoons. In each battalion was a special platoon for intervention which had firepower, mobility, and leadership ready to intervene at any moment. These vehicles, I presume from what I understand were used as a fire-fighting unit, as an intervention source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we say that they were fire-fighters putting out the fire?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: They were used for intervention at critical -- during a critical time in -- "fire-fighting" doesn't translate well literally into the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I will, for example, ask you -- you were in the operation zone Tomislavgrad on the level of the brigade regiment and lower. And you have the regiment who -- which needs assistance from the special assignment unit. How do you call them and what is the relationship with these units in the field itself? Who commands them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you would have to go for a request for that unit through the chain of command such as it existed, which means you would go to the -- from battalion level to brigade level, from brigade level to the zone level, and the zone would put in a request to -- depending whether it was an artillery unit, a so-called ATG unit, and they would approve or disapprove the request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when such a unit arrives to this battlefield, who will be commanding them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: If they are attached to that zone, they come under the overall command of the -- commander of the zone in that area of -- in his area of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us whether these so-called "ATGs" -- were these units which would hold front lines remaining there for a longer period of time, as they are called -- as you described them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would normally not do that, because they're not -- they're not formed -- the structure is not formed to hold the line. There are always exceptions to the rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where the -- the ATGs lived? Where were they housed? Where were they fed? Were they -- how were they organised? Were they seriously organised or not? What is your knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Could I ask this to be taken off the screen. I don't need this. I can follow the translation. They again were based at the municipal level, and they were based in their homes, like the majority of troops that I mentioned. They were probably in all likelihood they were younger men, physically fit, they had shown their mettle in a fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody coordinate? Was there any coordination between the ATGs? Was there any coordination or upper command, or did each and every municipality have its own ATG?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Could I just make a correction in the translation, one more. Not "medal" in a fight but "mettle."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question: Did each -- every municipality have its own ATG brigade? Was there any coordination among them, or how -- how were they directed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: In my unit, as I said, there was no such terminology used as an ATG.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But are you aware that in 1993, Mr. Mladen Naletilic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The witness just testified he has no personal knowledge or experience with an ATG.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I was listening very closely, I think I hear a leading question coming. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it is coming, but it's not realised yet. So I didn't know -- I just hear the name of the accused is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps an easier question: Do you know Mladen Naletilic? That would be a neutral question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to pose a question and then followed by this, what Your Honour said. I will ask you: Was there a Supreme Commander of all ATGs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1994 -- or the beginning of 1994, I believe such a man was put in a structure at the Ministry of Defence level. But before, I would say that I'm not aware that there was such an individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know a man, a person by the name of Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about him? Because we've been discussing about him here at length. But I -- I wanted first to clarify certain issues before -- during the direct examination. What do you know about Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I know he was born in Siroki Brijeg. I know that he was -- he was politically conscious of his country's situation. And I know he returned to Siroki Brijeg when the war started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any military functions?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you heard of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you know about the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I know of the battalion is that they were formed of previous political prisoners who had served time in the previous regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Could we have foundation for that. Is that based on personal knowledge or reading since the war or -- what's the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question is: Have you heard of the Convicts Battalion? He said, "Yes, I have." It means he has heard of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Then the answer goes on to say that he thinks it was formed by political -- sorry, I'm trying -- political prisoners. I'm just curious as to his basis for knowing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How do you know it was formed after previous political prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name interested me, so I asked in my headquarters, and this was explained to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any joint action undertaken with the Convicts Battalion there on the territory under your command?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: When I became commander in the summer of 1994, I worked -- excuse me, summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But this is already outside the scope of the indictment. I will not dwell on that. But maybe in 1993, did you undertake any action where the request was made for the Convicts Battalion to join in? And that was in 1993 I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, they were not in my zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where is the position of the Convicts Battalion in this structure? Did the command tell you when you asked? Was it a classical ATG? Who commands it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I imagine it would have a commander, if -- depending on the size of the unit. Again, I'm not sure of their size. If it was battalion size --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who heads it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, if he was attached to a unit in the -- to a zone, the final say in how it -- how the unit was used would be the zone commander. In 1994 or after the -- after the -- again, which is -- this is outside of the -- so I don't need to mention it. But --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But explain it, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: The structure changed, and all these smaller units were amalgamated into professional brigades in early 1994. So what I know remained of the Convicts Battalion was the 22nd Commando Section, which again was about company strength.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who was commanding -- commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC
utterances.text: I met -- yes. Then it was Andabak -- Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we -- it is now 7.00 p.m. We've completed this subject today. Tomorrow morning we will have another few questions for the witness. But for today, we have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I have to remind you, as I did other witnesses, that you are still under the solemn declaration. So do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I won't leave the hotel room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will rise until tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
